results.result: The manuscript provides epidemiological context for bladder cancer and upper tract urothelial carcinomas (UTUC), including incidence rates, the role of aristolochic acid exposure, and the high prevalence of UTUC in Taiwan.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C11 are all supported by appropriate citations to published epidemiological and clinical literature. These claims establish the background and public health significance of the study, providing context for the development of UroSEEK. The citations are to authoritative sources including the American Cancer Society, peer-reviewed journals, and cancer registries.

results.result: The manuscript describes the genetic landscape of urothelial cancers, including common mutations in TERT promoter, FGFR3, RAS, PIK3CA, TP53, CDKN2A, MLL, and ERBB2 genes in both bladder cancer and UTUC.
results.evaluation: Claims C12-C21 are well-supported by extensive citations to published literature characterizing the genetic alterations in urothelial cancers. These claims establish the scientific rationale for the gene panel selected for UroSEEK. The molecular mechanisms described (e.g., C15 regarding TERT promoter mutations) are supported by appropriate mechanistic studies.

results.result: The manuscript establishes the limitations of current diagnostic methods for urothelial cancers, including the poor sensitivity of urine cytology for low-grade tumors and UTUC, and the moderate performance of FDA-approved tests.
results.evaluation: Claims C22-C26 are supported by appropriate citations to published literature documenting the limitations of existing diagnostic approaches. These claims establish the clinical need for improved non-invasive detection methods, providing justification for the development of UroSEEK.

results.result: In the early detection cohort of 570 patients at risk for bladder cancer, UroSEEK detected 83% of patients who developed cancer, with specificity of 93% in at-risk patients and 99.5% in healthy controls. When combined with cytology, sensitivity increased to 95% with 93% specificity. UroSEEK positivity preceded clinical diagnosis by an average of 2.3 months.
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C28 and C62-C72 present the primary results from the early detection cohort with appropriate confidence intervals and statistical measures. The data demonstrate that UroSEEK substantially outperforms cytology alone (43% sensitivity) and that the combination achieves clinically meaningful performance. The temporal analysis (C65-C66) provides evidence for early detection capability. However, the specificity in at-risk patients (93%, C64) is lower than in healthy controls (99.5%, C63), which the authors acknowledge may reflect biological factors such as clonal proliferations.

results.result: The early detection cohort comprised 570 patients with median age 58 years, 70% male, 90% presenting with hematuria, with 31% developing bladder cancer after median follow-up of 18 months.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C37 describe the demographic and clinical characteristics of the early detection cohort. These are straightforward descriptive statistics supported by the study data. The gender distribution (C36) is consistent with published epidemiology of bladder cancer as noted by the authors.

results.result: The multiplex mutation assay detected mutations in 68% of urinary samples from patients who developed bladder cancer in the early detection cohort, with 246 mutations detected across eight genes. TP53 (45%) and FGFR3 (20%) were most commonly mutated. The assay showed high specificity: 1.7% false positive rate in at-risk patients without cancer and 0% in healthy controls.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C44 present the performance of the multiplex mutation component of UroSEEK with appropriate statistical measures. The mutation distribution (C41-C42) is consistent with known bladder cancer genetics. The high specificity in healthy controls (C44) and low false positive rate in at-risk patients (C43) support the technical validity of the assay. The median MAF of 8% (C40) indicates sufficient tumor DNA in urine samples.

results.result: TERT promoter mutations were detected in 57% of urinary samples from patients who developed bladder cancer in the early detection cohort, with 98% occurring at two known hotspot positions (g.1295228 and g.1295250). The assay showed 4% false positive rate in at-risk patients and near-zero rate in healthy controls.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C51 present the performance of the TERT promoter mutation component with appropriate statistical measures. The concentration of mutations at known hotspots (C47-C48) is consistent with published literature. The mechanistic explanation (C49) is supported by appropriate citation. The specificity data (C50-C51) demonstrate good technical performance, though slightly lower than the multiplex assay.

results.result: Aneuploidy was detected in 46% of urinary samples from patients who developed bladder cancer in the early detection cohort, with chromosome arms 5q, 8q, and 9p most commonly altered. The assay showed 1.5% false positive rate in at-risk patients and 0% in healthy controls.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C56 present the performance of the aneuploidy component with appropriate statistical measures. The chromosomes identified (C53) harbor known cancer genes (C54, supported by citation). The specificity is excellent in both control groups (C55-C56). The lower sensitivity (46%) compared to mutation assays is expected given the technical requirements for aneuploidy detection discussed later in the manuscript.

results.result: Analysis of primary tumor tissue from 102 patients showed that 89% contained mutations in at least one of the 11 genes, and 83% of mutations detected in urine were also found in the corresponding tumor. False negative urine tests were attributed to insufficient cancer cells in urine (62%) or absence of queried mutations in the tumor (38%).
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C61 provide important validation by comparing urine and tumor samples. The high concordance (C58) supports the biological validity of the urine-based assay. The analysis of false negatives (C59-C61) is logical and helps explain the sensitivity limitations. However, C60-C61 involve inference from the data rather than direct measurement, which introduces some uncertainty about the true causes of false negatives.

results.result: In the UTUC cohort of 56 patients, UroSEEK detected 75% of cases overall, including 79% of non-invasive (Ta/T1) tumors and 73% of muscle-invasive (T2-T4) tumors.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C30 and C100-C102 present the primary results from the UTUC cohort with appropriate confidence intervals. The similar sensitivity across tumor stages (C101-C102) is clinically important, suggesting the assay can detect early-stage disease. However, the UTUC cohort is relatively small (n=56), which limits the precision of these estimates and the ability to detect differences between subgroups.

results.result: The UTUC cohort consisted of 56 Taiwanese patients (32 females, 24 males) with atypical gender distribution compared to Western populations. Most had high-grade (89%) and muscle-invasive (66%) tumors, with 38% having synchronous bladder cancer. Renal function varied from unimpaired (45%) to severe disease (12%).
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C83 describe the demographic and clinical characteristics of the UTUC cohort. The atypical gender distribution (C74) is appropriately contextualized with citations showing consistency with AA-exposed populations. The clinical characteristics are straightforward descriptive statistics. The high proportion of high-grade and invasive tumors (C82-C83) may limit generalizability to early-stage UTUC detection.

results.result: The multiplex mutation assay detected mutations in 64% of urinary samples from UTUC patients, with 57 mutations across nine genes. TP53 (58%) and FGFR3 (16%) were most commonly mutated, with median MAF of 5.6%.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C88 present the mutation detection results in the UTUC cohort. The performance is similar to the bladder cancer cohort, supporting the applicability of UroSEEK to UTUC. The mutation distribution differs somewhat from bladder cancer (higher TP53, lower FGFR3), which is discussed in relation to ethnic differences and tumor grade distribution.

results.result: TERT promoter mutations were detected in 29% of urinary samples from UTUC patients, with 94% at the two main hotspots and median MAF of 2.22%.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C92 present the TERT promoter mutation results in the UTUC cohort. The lower sensitivity (29%) compared to bladder cancer (57%) may reflect biological differences, lower tumor DNA in urine, or the smaller sample size. The hotspot distribution (C91) is consistent with bladder cancer results.

results.result: Aneuploidy was detected in 39% of urinary samples from UTUC patients, with chromosome arms 1q, 7q, 8q, 17p, and 18q most commonly altered.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C94 present the aneuploidy results in the UTUC cohort. The sensitivity (39%) is similar to bladder cancer (46%). The chromosomes identified (C94) differ somewhat from bladder cancer, which may reflect biological differences between upper and lower tract tumors.

results.result: In UTUC patients, 90% of mutations detected in urine were also found in the corresponding tumor, and 96% of chromosomal alterations in urine were confirmed in tumors. False negative tests were primarily attributed to insufficient cancer cells in urine (76%).
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C99 provide validation by comparing urine and tumor samples in the UTUC cohort. The high concordance (C95-C97) supports biological validity. The analysis of false negatives (C98-C99) is logical but involves inference. The authors acknowledge that multiple tumors per patient and intratumoral heterogeneity may explain some discrepancies, which is an important caveat.

results.result: In the UTUC cohort, cytology was positive in only 9.5% of cases, while UroSEEK detected all cytology-positive cases plus additional cases. UroSEEK raised cytology sensitivity from 10% to 75%. For low-grade UTUC, UroSEEK detected 80% while cytology detected none.
results.evaluation: Claims C103-C106, C145-C146 demonstrate the substantial advantage of UroSEEK over cytology for UTUC detection. The very low cytology sensitivity (9.5%, C103) highlights the clinical need for improved detection methods. The performance in low-grade UTUC (C146) is particularly important for early detection. However, the small number of cytology-positive cases (4/42) limits the precision of these comparisons.

results.result: All but two UTUC patients had detectable aristolactam-DNA adducts in renal cortex (range 0.4-68 adducts per 10^8 nucleotides), and the A>T mutational signature characteristic of aristolochic acid was highly represented in TP53 (18/32) and HRAS (2/2) mutations found in urinary cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C107-C110 provide strong evidence for aristolochic acid exposure in the UTUC cohort through both DNA adduct measurements (C107-C108) and mutational signatures (C109-C110). The mechanistic explanation (C110) is supported by appropriate citations. This validates the cohort selection and provides biological context for the high UTUC incidence in Taiwan.

results.result: In the surveillance cohort of 322 patients with prior bladder cancer, UroSEEK detected 68% of patients who developed recurrence, with 80% specificity. UroSEEK positivity preceded clinical diagnosis by an average of 7 months, with 47 cases detected more than one year in advance.
results.evaluation: Claims C31, C128-C131 present the primary results from the surveillance cohort. The sensitivity (68%, C128) is lower than in the early detection cohort (83%), which may reflect differences in tumor biology, treatment effects, or the challenge of detecting recurrence. The specificity (80%, C129) is also lower than in early detection (93%), which the authors discuss in terms of possible clonal proliferations. The temporal analysis (C130-C131) demonstrates potential for early detection of recurrence.

results.result: The surveillance cohort comprised 322 patients with prior bladder cancer containing mutations in at least one of the 11 genes, with median age 62 years and 75% male. 58% developed recurrence after median follow-up of 10.7 months.
results.evaluation: Claims C111-C114 describe the surveillance cohort characteristics. The selection criterion (tumor with mutation in at least one gene, C111) introduces potential bias by excluding patients whose tumors lack these mutations, which may affect generalizability. The demographic characteristics (C113-C114) are consistent with bladder cancer epidemiology.

results.result: The multiplex mutation assay detected mutations in 52% of urinary samples from patients who developed recurrent bladder cancer, with FGFR3 (43%) and TP53 (30%) most commonly mutated. 7% of patients without recurrence had detectable mutations. Mean lead time was 7 months.
results.evaluation: Claims C115-C120 present the multiplex mutation results in the surveillance cohort. The sensitivity (52%, C115) is lower than in early detection (68%), which may reflect biological differences in recurrent tumors or treatment effects. The shift toward FGFR3 mutations (C117) compared to early detection is interesting and may reflect the biology of recurrent disease. The 7% false positive rate (C119) is higher than in early detection, which the authors acknowledge.

results.result: TERT promoter mutations were detected in 57% of urinary samples from patients who developed recurrent bladder cancer, with median MAF of 5%. 10% of patients without recurrence had detectable TERT mutations. Mean lead time was 7 months.
results.evaluation: Claims C121-C124 present the TERT promoter mutation results in the surveillance cohort. The sensitivity (57%, C121) is similar to early detection, suggesting TERT mutations remain a good biomarker for recurrence. The 10% false positive rate (C124) is higher than in early detection (4%), which may reflect clonal proliferations or very early recurrences not yet clinically detectable.

results.result: Aneuploidy was detected in 28% of urinary samples from patients who developed recurrent bladder cancer, with chromosome arms 8p, 8q, and 9p most commonly altered. Only 2% of patients without recurrence showed aneuploidy.
results.evaluation: Claims C125-C127 present the aneuploidy results in the surveillance cohort. The sensitivity (28%, C125) is lower than in early detection (46%), which may reflect lower tumor burden in recurrent disease. The very low false positive rate (2%, C127) suggests aneuploidy is a highly specific marker for recurrence.

results.result: In the surveillance cohort, cytology detected 25% of recurrent cancers with 100% specificity. UroSEEK detected 90% of cytology-positive cases and 61% of cytology-negative cases. Combined, UroSEEK plus cytology achieved 71% sensitivity and 82% specificity, raising cytology sensitivity from 25% to 71%.
results.evaluation: Claims C132-C137, C144 demonstrate the complementary value of UroSEEK and cytology in surveillance. The improvement in sensitivity (C136, C144) is clinically meaningful. However, the specificity of the combination (82%, C137) is lower than cytology alone (100%, C133), which reflects the UroSEEK false positives. The authors acknowledge this trade-off in the discussion.

results.result: Across both cohorts, UroSEEK detected 67% of low-grade bladder cancers while cytology detected none (0/49). For high-grade tumors, UroSEEK detected 80% compared to 45% for cytology. UroSEEK raised cytology sensitivity from 43% to 95% in the early detection cohort.
results.evaluation: Claims C32, C138-C141, C143 demonstrate the particular advantage of UroSEEK for low-grade tumors, where cytology has essentially no sensitivity. This is clinically important because low-grade tumors, while less aggressive, still require monitoring and treatment. The performance on high-grade tumors (C140-C141) shows UroSEEK also improves detection of more aggressive disease. The combined sensitivity improvement (C143) is substantial and clinically meaningful.

results.result: All 51 patients with cytology-positive urine in the early detection cohort developed biopsy-proven bladder cancer, confirming cytology's high specificity. Among 105 cases with atypical cytology, 19% developed cancer. UroSEEK was positive in 95% of atypical cases that developed cancer but only 13% of atypical cases that did not.
results.evaluation: Claims C142, C147-C150 demonstrate the value of UroSEEK for resolving equivocal cytology results. The 100% positive predictive value of positive cytology (C142) confirms its specificity. The ability to discriminate among atypical cases (C149-C150) is clinically valuable, as atypical cytology is common and creates diagnostic uncertainty. This represents an important potential clinical application of UroSEEK.

results.result: In a comparison of matched urine and plasma samples from 14 UTUC patients, mutations were detected in 93% of urinary cell DNA samples but only 36% of plasma samples. The plasma test failed to identify any of six non-muscle-invasive cancers, while all were detected in urine. Median MAF was 0.3% in plasma versus 15% in urinary cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C151-C153 provide important evidence supporting the choice of urinary cells over plasma for urothelial cancer detection. The substantial enrichment of tumor DNA in urine (C153) explains the superior performance. However, this comparison is limited by small sample size (n=14) and was performed on UTUC patients only. The failure to detect non-muscle-invasive cancers in plasma (C152) is particularly important for early detection applications.

results.result: Based on published prevalence estimates (2.4-31.1% with microscopic hematuria, 5% with urothelial cancer) and the study's performance data (95% sensitivity, 93% specificity), UroSEEK plus cytology extrapolates to 66% positive predictive value and 99.3% negative predictive value for bladder cancer in patients with microscopic hematuria or dysuria.
results.evaluation: Claims C154-C156 involve extrapolation from the study data to a clinical population. While the calculations appear mathematically sound (C156), they rely on prevalence estimates from other studies (C154-C155) and assume the study cohort is representative of the target clinical population. The wide range of hematuria prevalence (2.4-31.1%, C154) introduces substantial uncertainty. Additionally, the study cohort was enriched for cancer cases (31% vs. 5% expected), which may affect the generalizability of the performance estimates. These predictions require prospective validation in an unselected clinical population.

results.result: A mutation in at least one of the 11 queried genes was present in 95.2% of bladder cancers evaluated in the study.
results.evaluation: Claim C157 is supported by the study's tumor analysis data. This high frequency justifies the gene panel selection and suggests the assay has broad applicability. However, it also means that approximately 5% of bladder cancers lack mutations in these genes and would not be detectable by the mutation components of UroSEEK, though they might still be detected by aneuploidy.

results.result: Published survival data show that 91% of stage T1 UTUC patients are cured by surgery, compared to 78%, 34%, and 0% for stages T2, T3, and T4 respectively.
results.evaluation: Claims C158-C161 are supported by citation to Li et al., 2008. These data provide clinical context for the importance of early UTUC detection, as survival is dramatically better for early-stage disease. This justifies the focus on detecting non-invasive tumors.

results.result: Published estimates indicate that 100 million people in China are at risk for UTUC due to aristolochic acid exposure. UTUC recurrence occurs in the bladder in 22-47% of cases and in the contralateral tract in 2-6% of cases (up to 30% in AA-related UTUC).
results.evaluation: Claims C162-C165 are supported by appropriate citations to published epidemiological and clinical data. These claims establish the public health significance of UTUC, particularly in AA-exposed populations, and the clinical need for surveillance methods to detect recurrence.

results.result: Urine cytology failed to detect 90% of UTUC cases in the current study.
results.evaluation: Claim C166 is directly supported by the study's data showing cytology detected only 9.5% (4/42) of UTUC cases. This dramatic failure of cytology for UTUC detection highlights the clinical need for alternative methods.

results.result: False positives have been observed in all other molecular assays for bladder cancer, including FDA-approved tests.
results.evaluation: Claim C167 is supported by citations to published studies documenting false positives in other bladder cancer tests. This provides context for interpreting the false positive rates observed with UroSEEK and suggests this is a general challenge in the field rather than a specific limitation of UroSEEK.

results.result: Simulations and published data indicate that DNA containing a minimum of 1% neoplastic cells is required for reliable aneuploidy detection, while mutations can be detected in as few as 0.03% of DNA templates.
results.evaluation: Claims C168-C169 are supported by the study's own simulations and citations to published literature on detection limits. This explains why the mutation assays have higher sensitivity than the aneuploidy assay and provides technical context for interpreting the results. The 1% threshold for aneuploidy (C168) is a significant limitation that may explain some false negatives.

results.result: The cost of managing bladder cancer patients under surveillance is in aggregate higher than the cost of managing any other type of cancer, amounting to 3 billion dollars annually.
results.evaluation: Claim C170 is supported by citation to Netto and Epstein, 2010. This provides economic context for the potential value of UroSEEK in reducing surveillance costs by potentially reducing the frequency of cystoscopy.

results.result: The cost of UroSEEK plus cytology is estimated to be less than 1/3 of the cost of cystoscopy.
results.evaluation: Claim C171 is based on the authors' estimation rather than formal cost analysis. While plausible, this claim lacks supporting data or methodology. The actual cost-effectiveness of UroSEEK would depend on many factors including test costs, cystoscopy costs, the clinical algorithm for using the test, and the consequences of false positives and false negatives. A formal cost-effectiveness analysis would be needed to support this claim.

results.result: Clonal proliferations that are not considered neoplastic have been described in bone, skin, and other tissues.
results.evaluation: Claim C172 is supported by citation to Risques and Kennedy, 2018. The authors use this to speculate about possible explanations for false positive results, suggesting that age-related clonal proliferations in bladder epithelium might harbor mutations detectable by UroSEEK without representing true cancer. This is a reasonable hypothesis but remains speculative in the context of bladder epithelium.

results.result: The distribution of mutant genes in UTUC tumors was consistent with some published studies but not others. TP53 mutations were found only in high-grade UTUC while FGFR3 mutations dominated in low-grade tumors (5/6). The overall FGFR3 mutation frequency (21%) was lower than some Western studies (54-74%) but comparable to Asian studies (8-13%), attributed to ethnic differences.
results.evaluation: Claims C173-C177 provide important context for interpreting the UTUC mutation data. The comparison with published literature (C173, C176-C177) is appropriately nuanced, acknowledging both consistencies and discrepancies. The ethnic differences in FGFR3 mutation frequency (C177) are supported by citation and provide a plausible explanation for the lower frequency observed. The grade-specific mutation patterns (C174-C175) are consistent with bladder cancer biology.

results.result: UroSEEK incorporates massive parallel sequencing assays for mutations in 11 genes (FGFR3, TP53, CDKN2A, ERBB2, HRAS, KRAS, PIK3CA, MET, VHL, MLL) and copy number changes on 39 chromosome arms, with three components: a 10-gene multiplex assay, TERT promoter mutation detection, and aneuploidy detection.
results.evaluation: Claims C178-C179 describe the technical design of UroSEEK. These are supported by the methods section and appropriate citations for each component. The gene selection is justified by published literature on urothelial cancer genetics. The three-component design is logical and takes advantage of different types of genetic alterations.

results.result: Urine samples were collected prospectively from patients in four institutions across multiple countries. The study was approved by institutional review boards. A minimum of 12 months follow-up was required for patients without cancer.
results.evaluation: Claims C180-C182 describe the study design and ethical oversight. The multi-institutional, international design (C180) strengthens generalizability. The IRB approval (C181) confirms ethical conduct. The 12-month follow-up requirement (C182) is reasonable for establishing true negative status, though longer follow-up would be preferable to rule out very slow-growing tumors.
